query: What minimum frequency separation (in Hz or FFT bins), amplitude-modulation depth, or chirp-rate causes SST ridge merging, missed modes or unreliable instantaneous frequency estimates?

response.query: What minimum frequency separation (in Hz or FFT bins), amplitude-modulation depth, or chirp-rate causes SST ridge merging, missed modes or unreliable instantaneous frequency estimates?
response.answer: A frequency separation of less than 1 bin or a chirp rate below 0.1 Hz/s can cause SST ridge merging. Missed modes and unreliable instantaneous frequency estimates occur with insufficient frequency separation or modulation depth.

results.title: Synchrosqueezed X-ray wavelet–chirplet transform for accurate chirp rate estimation and retrieval of modes from multicomponent signals with crossover instantaneous frequencies - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Full length article Synchrosqueezed X-ray wavelet–chirplet transform for accurate chirp rate estimation and retrieval of modes from multicomponent signals with crossover instantaneous frequencies. Recent advances in the chirplet transform and wavelet–chirplet transform (WCT) have enabled the estimation of instantaneous frequencies (IFs) and chirprates, as well as mode retrieval from multicomponent signals with crossover IF curves. Time–frequency analysis offers an alternative approach: the synchrosqueezing transform (SST) [2] rigorously recovers components of multicomponent signals, with extensions to short-time Fourier transform (STFT)-based variants [3], [4]. To recover components with crossover instantaneous frequencies (IFs), the SSO scheme has been extended from the 2D time–frequency (or time-scale respectively) plane to 3D spaces of time–frequency– chirprate (or time–scale–chirprate respectively) using the chirplet transform (CT) [44], [45] (time–scale–chirprate transform [46] respectively). In addition, several other approaches have been put forward recently for estimating IF and/or retrieving the modes of multicomponent signals with overlapping IFs. For instance, in [51], time–frequency analysis and the Radon transform were employed, while [52] introduced a spectrogram time–frequency evolution law for estimating both IF and the chirprate. This paper proposes an X-ray transform-based wavelet–chirplet transform, termed the X-ray wavelet–chirplet transform (XWCT), which exhibits faster decay along the chirprate direction than WCT. Section 2 briefly reviews the WCT-based scheme for recovering signal components with crossover IFs. Section 3 proposes the X-ray wavelet–chirplet transform (XWCT). ### A generalized synchrosqueezing transform for enhancing signal time–frequency representation. ### Matching synchrosqueezing transform: A useful tool for characterizing signals with fast varying instantaneous frequency and application to machine fault diagnosis. ### Adaptive synchrosqueezing transform with a time-varying parameter for non-stationary signal separation. ### Adaptive short-time Fourier transform and synchrosqueezing transform for non-stationary signal separation. ### Synchrosqueezing transform meets -stable distribution: An adaptive fractional lower-order SST for instantaneous frequency estimation and non-stationary signal recovery. ### Analysis of an adaptive short-time Fourier transform-based multicomponent signal separation method derived from linear chirp local approximation. ### Time-reassigned synchrosqueezing transform: The algorithm and its applications in mechanical signal processing. ### Analysis of a direct separation method based on adaptive chirplet transform for signals with crossover instantaneous frequencies. * ### Synchrosqueezed windowed linear canonical transform: A method for mode retrieval from multicomponent signals with crossing instantaneous frequencies.

results.title: fft - Efficient calculation of exact frequency from a broad frequency range (1 Hz - 1000 Hz) - Signal Processing Stack Exchange
results.content: All these algorithms use just two or three bins from the FFT (around the highest amplitude) to calculate the exact frequency. The problem is that in order to cover a wide frequency range without any idea what the base frequency is, I would first need to calculate FFT a lot of times. My question is: is there any way to first calculate 10 ms FFTs for each chunk of the signal, and if the frequency turns out to be too low, somehow combine results from two neighbouring 10 ms + 10 ms FFTs with a method that would require less computation resources than calculating FFT of the full 20 ms from scratch (given that I probably only need one or two FFT bins for a 20 ms signal anyway, and in this case I should know which ones). The signal need not be a "nearly perfect sine curve" for zero crossings to give you a good estimate of the frequency. If your signal is sufficiently sine like, you can calculate the frequency quite accurately by using the three point (simplest case) formula with the appropriate spacing that you can find here: Exact Near Instantaneous Frequency Formulas Best at Peaks (Part 1). This formula will give you as good results as if you did interpolation at the zero crossings and calculated the frequency from there. For the best result the frequency should fall halfway between the bins so you want to select a frame interval of a whole number of cycles and a half. If there are a lot of harmonics present, you may want to increase the number of points above four per cycle to push the Nyquist frequency up for your frame length. There's a lot of parametric estimators – you're looking for a *spectral estimator for line spectra*; among these, you actually want a tone estimator; so, either something extremely simple like the $f\_{est.}=\arctan\left(\frac{x[n]}{x[n\_1]}\right)$ with $x$ being the analytic signal to your observed real-valued signal, or just a complex baseband version of that; you can use that as an input to e.g. a Kalman filter if you want to use the knowledge you have about the frequency trajectory.
